419279 read(10, "# This file defines a single function for booting a package set from a list of\n# stages. The exact mechanics of that function are defined below; here I\n# (@Ericson2314) wish to describe the purpose of the abstraction.\n#\n# The first goal is consistency across stdenvs. Regardless of what this function\n# does, by making every stdenv use it for bootstrapping we ensure that they all\n# work in a similar way. [Before this abstraction, each stdenv was its own\n# special snowflake due to different authors writing in different times.]\n#\n# The second goal is consistency across each stdenv's stage functions. By\n# writing each stage in terms of the previous stage, commonalities between them\n# are more easily observable. [Before, there usually was a big attribute set\n# with each stage, and stages would access the previous stage by name.]\n#\n# The third goal is composition. Because each stage is written in terms of the\n# previous, the list can be reordered or, more practically, extended with new\n# stages. The latter is used for cross compiling and custom\n# stdenvs. Additionally, certain options should by default apply only to the\n# last stage, whatever it may be. By delaying the creation of stage package sets\n# until the final fold, we prevent these options from inhibiting composition.\n#\n# The fourth and final goal is debugging. Normal packages should only source\n# their dependencies from the current stage. But for the sake of debugging, it\n# is nice that all packages still remain accessible. We make sure previous\n# stages are kept around with a `stdenv.__bootPackages` attribute referring the\n# previous stage. It is idiomatic that attributes prefixed with `__` come with\n# special restrictions and should not be used under normal circumstances.\n{ lib, allPackages }:\n\n# Type:\n#   [ pkgset -> (args to stage/default.nix) or ({ __raw = true; } // pkgs) ]\n#   -> pkgset\n#\n# In English: This takes a list of function from the previous stage pkgset and\n# returns the final pkgset. Each of those functions returns, if `__raw` is\n# undefined or false, args for this stage's pkgset (the most complex and\n# important arg is the stdenv), or, if `__raw = true`, simply this stage's\n# pkgset itself.\n#\n# The list takes stages in order, so the final stage is last in the list. In\n# other words, this does a foldr not foldl.\nstageFuns:\nlet\n\n  /*\n    \"dfold\" a ternary function `op' between successive elements of `list' as if\n    it was a doubly-linked list with `lnul' and `rnul` base cases at either\n    end. In precise terms, `dfold op lnul rnul [x_0 x_1 x_2 ... x_n-1]` is the\n    same as\n\n      let\n        f_-1  = lnul f_0;\n        f_0   = op f_-1   x_0  f_1;\n        f_1   = op f_0    x_1  f_2;\n        f_2   = op f_1    x_2  f_3;\n        ...\n        f_n   = op f_n-1  x_n  f_n+1;\n        f_n+1 = rnul f_n;\n      in\n        f_0\n  */\n  dfold =\n    op: lnul: rnul: list:\n    let\n      len = builtins.length list;\n      go =\n        pred: n:\n        if n == len then\n          rnul pred\n        else\n          let\n            # Note the cycle -- call-by-need ensures finite fold.\n            cur = op pred (builtins.elemAt list n) succ;\n            succ = go cur (n + 1);\n          in\n          cur;\n      lapp = lnul cur;\n      cur = go lapp 0;\n    in\n    cur;\n\n  # Take the list and disallow custom overrides in all but the final stage,\n  # and allow it in the final flag. If we hit this\n        # code here, we'll cause an infinite recursion. Since a set with\n        # clang as its default compiler always means libc++, we can infer this\n        # decision statically.\n        then\n          buildPackages.pkgsBuildTarget.llvmPackages.libcxxClang\n        else\n          buildPackages.gcc\n      else\n        # This will blow up if anything uses it, but that's OK. The `if\n        # buildPackages.stdenv.cc.isClang then ... else ...` would blow up\n        # everything, so we make sure to avoid that.\n        buildPackages.stdenv.cc;\n  };\n\n  pkgs = dfold folder postStage (_: { }) withAllowCustomOverrides;\n\nin\n# Return the spliced package set, so that consumers of the nixpkgs top-level\n# attributes, like NixOS, don't break when cross-compiling.\npkgs.__splicedPackages\n", 6679) = 6679

419279 read(10, "# This file turns the pkgs/by-name directory (see its README.md for more info) into an overlay that adds all the defined packages.\n# No validity checks are done here,\n# instead this file is optimised for performance,\n# and validity checks are done by CI on PRs.\n\n# Type: Path -> Overlay\nbaseDirectory:\nlet\n  # Because of Nix's import-value cache, importing lib is free\n  lib = import ../../lib;\n\n  inherit (builtins)\n    readDir\n    ;\n\n  inherit (lib.attrsets)\n    mapAttrs\n    mapAttrsToList\n    mergeAttrsList\n    ;\n\n  # Package files for a single shard\n  # Type: String -> String -> AttrsOf Path\n  namesForShard =\n    shard: type:\n    if type != \"directory\" then\n      # Ignore all non-directories. Technically only README.md is allowed as a file in the base directory, so we could alternatively:\n      # - Assume that README.md is the only file and change the condition to `shard == \"README.md\"` for a minor performance improvement.\n      #   This would however cause very poor error messages if there's other files.\n      # - Ensure that README.md is the only file, throwing a better error message if that's not the case.\n      #   However this would make for a poor code architecture, because one type of error would have to be duplicated in the validity checks and here.\n      # Additionally in either of those alternatives, we would have to duplicate the hardcoding of \"README.md\"\n      { }\n    else\n      mapAttrs (name: _: baseDirectory + \"/${shard}/${name}/package.nix\") (\n        readDir (baseDirectory + \"/${shard}\")\n      );\n\n  # The attribute set mapping names to the package files defining them\n  # This is defined up here in order to allow reuse of the value (it's kind of expensive to compute)\n  # if the overlay has to be applied multiple times\n  packageFiles = mergeAttrsList (mapAttrsToList namesForShard (readDir baseDirectory));\nin\nself: super:\n{\n  # This attribute is necessary to allow CI to ensure that all packages defined in `pkgs/by-name`\n  # don't have an overriding definition in `all-packages.nix` with an empty (`{ }`) second `callPackage` argument.\n  # It achieves that with an overlay that modifies both `callPackage` and this attribute to signal whether `callPackage` is used\n  # and whether it's defined by this file here or `all-packages.nix`.\n  # TODO: This can be removed once `pkgs/by-name` can handle custom `callPackage` arguments without `all-packages.nix` (or any other way of achieving the same result).\n  # Because at that point the code in ./stage.nix can be changed to not allow definitions in `all-packages.nix` to override ones from `pkgs/by-name` anymore and throw an error if that happens instead.\n  _internalCallByNamePackageFile = file: self.callPackage file { };\n}\n// mapAttrs (name: self._internalCallByNamePackageFile) packageFiles\n", 2790) = 2790

419279 read(10, "# The `splicedPackages' package set, and its use by `callPackage`\n#\n# The `buildPackages` pkg set is a new concept, and the vast majority package\n# expression (the other *.nix files) are not designed with it in mind. This\n# presents us with a problem with how to get the right version (build-time vs\n# run-time) of a package to a consumer that isn't used to thinking so cleverly.\n#\n# The solution is to splice the package sets together as we do below, so every\n# `callPackage`d expression in fact gets both versions. The `actuallySplice`\n# parameter there the boolean value of that equality check.\nlib: pkgs: actuallySplice:\n\nlet\n  inherit (lib.customisation) mapCrossIndex renameCrossIndexFrom;\n  inherit (lib) mapAttrs;\n\n  spliceReal =\n    inputs:\n    let\n      mash =\n        # Other pkgs sets\n        inputs.buildBuild\n        // inputs.buildTarget\n        // inputs.hostHost\n        // inputs.targetTarget\n        # The same pkgs sets one probably intends\n        // inputs.buildHost\n        // inputs.hostTarget;\n      merge =\n        name: defaultValue:\n        let\n          # `or {}` is for the non-derivation attsert splicing case, where `{}` is the identity.\n          value' = mapCrossIndex (x: x.${name} or { }) inputs;\n\n          augmentedValue = defaultValue // {\n            __spliced = lib.filterAttrs (k: v: inputs.${k} ? ${name}) value';\n          };\n          # Get the set of outputs of a derivation. If one derivation fails to\n          # evaluate we don't want to diverge the entire splice, so we fall back\n          # on {}\n          tryGetOutputs =\n            value0:\n            let\n              inherit (builtins.tryEval value0) success value;\n            in\n            getOutputs (lib.optionalAttrs success value);\n          getOutputs =\n            value: lib.genAttrs (value.outputs or (lib.optional (value ? out) \"out\")) (output: value.${output});\n          outputNames = defaultValue.outputs or (lib.optional (defaultValue ? out) \"out\");\n          outputSplice = spliceReal (\n            mapCrossIndex tryGetOutputs value' // { hostTarget = getOutputs value'.hostTarget; }\n          );\n        in\n        # The derivation along with its outputs, which we recur\n        # on to splice them together.\n        if lib.isDerivation defaultValue then\n          augmentedValue // lib.genAttrs outputNames (out: outputSplice.${out})\n        else if lib.isAttrs defaultValue then\n          spliceReal value'\n        else\n          # Don't be fancy about non-derivations. 419279 read(10, "# The Nixpkgs CC is not directly usable, since it doesn't know where\n# the C library and standard header files are. Therefore the compiler\n# produced by that package cannot be installed directly in a user\n# environment and used from the command line. So we use a wrapper\n# script that sets up the right environment variables so that the\n# compiler and the linker just \"work\".\n\n{\n  name ? \"\",\n  lib,\n  stdenvNoCC,\n  runtimeShell,\n  cc ? null,\n  libc ? null,\n  bintools,\n  coreutils ? null,\n  apple-sdk ? null,\n  nativeTools,\n  noLibc ? false,\n  nativeLibc,\n  nativePrefix ? \"\",\n  propagateDoc ? cc != null && cc ? man,\n  extraTools ? [ ],\n  extraPackages ? [ ],\n  extraBuildCommands ? \"\",\n  nixSupport ? { },\n  isGNU ? false,\n  isClang ? cc.isClang or false,\n  isZig ? cc.isZig or false,\n  isArocc ? cc.isArocc or false,\n  isCcache ? cc.isCcache or false,\n  gnugrep ? null,\n  expand-response-params,\n  libcxx ? null,\n\n  # Whether or not to add `-B` and `-L` to `nix-support/cc-{c,ld}flags`\n  useCcForLibs ?\n\n    # Always add these flags for Clang, because in order to compile (most\n    # software) it needs libraries that are shipped and compiled with gcc.\n    if isClang then\n      true\n\n    # Never add these flags for a build!=host cross-compiler or a host!=target\n    # (\"cross-built-native\") compiler; currently nixpkgs has a special build\n    # path for these (`crossStageStatic`). In spite of all this effort we still can't be sure of our\n    ability to reproduce the binary bootstrap-files, since the\n    compilers that built them don't always produce exactly bit-for-bit\n    deterministic results.\n\n    Since this archive contains no binaries and uses a format (NAR)\n    specifically designed for bit-exact reproducibility, none of the\n    requirements above apply to `minimal-bootstrap-sources`.\n  */\n  minimal-bootstrap-sources = derivation {\n    inherit name;\n    system = hostPlatform.system;\n    outputHashMode = \"recursive\";\n    inherit outputHashAlgo outputHash;\n\n    # This builder always fails, but fortunately Nix will print the\n    # \"builder\", which is really the error message that we want the\n    # user to see.\n    builder = ''\n      #\n      #\n      # Neither your store nor your substituters seems to have:\n      #\n      #  ${placeholder \"out\"}\n      #\n      # You can create this path from an already-bootstrapped nixpkgs\n      # using the following command:\n      #\n      #   nix-build '<nixpkgs>' -A make-minimal-bootstrap-sources\n      #\n      # Or, if you prefer, you can create this file using only `git`,\n      # `nix`, and `xz`. Summary\nAdd a permission case system with required caller context and paged evidence display for write/patch/shell operations in restricted mode.\n\n## Context\nWhen using forge in restricted mode, the permission approval flow had three problems:\n\n1. **No context at decision time**: The TUI permission prompt cleared the terminal, erasing all context about what was being approved\n2. **No caller justification**: Write/patch operations had no way to carry the LLM's reasoning or justification through to the permission prompt\n3. **No evidence inspection**: Users had no way to inspect the full proposed diff before making a decision \342\200\224 only a truncated single-line message was visible\n\nThis implements a judicial-style evidence collection system where every decision point is preceded by a full case brief showing what changed, why, and where to find the full details.\n\n## Changes\n\n### Permission Case System (new: `crates/forge_domain/src/policies/case.rs`)\n- `PermissionCase` struct collects all decision evidence: case_id, timestamp, operation type, file path, proposed changes, and caller explanation\n- Atomic counter ensures unique case IDs across rapid sequential decisions\n- `format_panel()` renders a styled evidence panel for display\n- Tests verify case creation, ID uniqueness, panel rendering, and patch diff display\n\n### Required `context` field on tool calls (`crates/forge_domain/src/tools/catalog.rs`)\n- `FSWrite`, `FSPatch`, `FSMultiPatch` now require a `context: String` field\n- The LLM must provide a justification for every write/patch (enforced via JSON schema, no `#[serde(default)]`)\n- `Shell` also requires `context: String` for command reasoning\n- `CommandType` enum classifies shell commands: `InlineCode` (here-docs, eval, embedded scripts \342\200\224 auto-denied), `FileScript`, `Utility`\n- All snapshots and test fixtures updated for the new schema\n\n### Paged evidence display (`crates/forge_app/src/tool_registry.rs`)\n- `build_case()` constructs the full case from tool input, collecting untruncated content\n- `print_case()` writes the case brief to `/tmp/forge-cases/<case_id>.md` and pipes it through `less` (respects `$PAGER` env)\n- After the user quits the pager, the TUI permission prompt appears\n- `check_tool_permission()` appends the case file path to the TUI message for later reference\n- Inline-code shell commands are auto-denied before reaching the TUI\n- Full untruncated diffs shown (removed 120-char truncation limits since content is now paged)\n\n### Permission operation message field (`crates/forge_domain/src/policies/operation.rs`)\n- `PermissionOperation::Execute` now carries a `message: String` for classification info\n- All pattern matches updated (`policy.rs`, `rule.rs`, `engine.rs`)\n\n### `fmt_input.rs` enhancements\n- Write/Patch/MultiPatch tool input display now shows proposed content/diff inline\n\n## Use Cases\n- **Write approval**: See full file content in `less` before allowing the write\n- **Patch approval**: Scroll through the complete old\342\206\222new diff in the pager before deciding\n- **Shell execution**: See the command type classification (auto-deny inline code)\n- **Audit trail**: Every permission decision has a case file in `/tmp/forge-cases/` with full evidence\n\n## The system should support user registration, login, logout, and token refresh capabilities while maintaining security best practices.\n\n## Implementation Plan\n\n- [ ] 1. Set up authentication dependencies and configuration\n  - Add JWT library (e.g., jsonwebtoken) and bcrypt for password hashing\n  - Configure environment variables for JWT secrets and token expiration\n  - Rationale: Establishes foundation for secure authentication\n  - Dependencies: None - this is the first step\n\n- [ ] 2. Create user model and database schema\n  - Define User entity with fields: id, email, password_hash, created_at, updated_at\n  - Add unique constraint on email field\n  - Create database migration for users table\n  - Rationale: Provides data structure for storing user credentials\n  - Dependencies: Database connection must be configured\n\n- [ ] 3. Implement password hashing service\n  - Create service to hash passwords using bcrypt with appropriate salt rounds\n  - Add password verification function\n  - Include unit tests for hashing and verification\n  - Rationale: Ensures passwords are never stored in plain text\n  - Dependencies: User model must exist\n\n- [ ] 4. Build JWT token generation and validation\n  - Create service to generate JWT tokens with user claims\n  - Implement token verification and decoding logic\n  - Add refresh token functionality with longer expiration\n  - Rationale: Enables stateless authentication and session management\n  - Dependencies: User model and environment configuration\n\n- [ ] 5. Create authentication endpoints\n  - POST /auth/register - User registration with email/password\n  - POST /auth/login - User login returning access and refresh tokens\n  - POST /auth/logout - Invalidate user session\n  - POST /auth/refresh - Generate new access token from refresh token\n  - Rationale: Provides API interface for authentication operations\n  - Dependencies: All services from previous steps\n\n- [ ] 6. Implement authentication middleware\n  - Create middleware to validate JWT tokens on protected routes\n  - Extract user information from valid tokens\n  - Return 401 for invalid or expired tokens\n  - Rationale: Protects routes requiring authentication\n  - Dependencies: JWT validation service\n\n- [ ] 7. Add rate limiting for authentication endpoints\n  - Implement rate limiting on login and registration endpoints\n  - Configure appropriate limits (e.g., 5 attempts per 15 minutes)\n  - Rationale: Prevents brute force attacks\n  - Dependencies: Authentication endpoints must exist\n\n- [ ] 8. Write integration tests for authentication flow\n  - Test complete registration \342\206\222 login \342\206\222 access protected route flow\n  - Test token refresh mechanism\n  - Test error cases (invalid credentials, expired tokens)\n  - Rationale: Ensures entire authentication system works correctly\n  - Dependencies: All implementation steps complete\n\n## Verification Criteria\n\n- User can successfully register with valid email and password\n- User can login and receive valid JWT tokens\n- Protected routes return 401 for unauthenticated requests\n- Protected routes allow access with valid JWT token\n- Tokens expire after configured duration\n- Refresh tokens can generate new access tokens\n- Passwords are hashed and never stored in plain text\n- Rate limiting prevents excessive authentication attempts\n- All unit and integration tests pass\n- Security audit shows no critical vulnerabilities\n\n## Potential Risks and Mitigations\n\n1. **Token Secret Exposure**\n   - Impact: If JWT secret is exposed, attackers can forge valid tokens\n   - Likelihood: Medium\n   - Mitigation: Store secrets in environment variables, never commit to repository, rotate secrets periodically\n   - Contingency: Implement secret rotation mechanism and token revocation list\n\n2. **Weak Password Policy**\n   - Impact: Users choose weak passwords that are easily compromised\n   - Likelihood: High\n   - Mitigation: Enforce minimum password requirements (length, complexity), implement password strength meter\n   - Contingency: Add option to require password reset for weak passwords\n\n3. **Session Hijacking**\n   - Impact: Attacker steals valid token and impersonates user\n   - Likelihood: Medium\n   - Mitigation: Use HTTPS only, implement short token expiration, add IP address validation\n   - Contingency: Implement token revocation and force logout capability\n\n4. **Brute Force Attacks**\n   - Impact: Attacker attempts many password combinations to gain access\n   - Likelihood: High\n   - Mitigation: Implement rate limiting, add CAPTCHA after failed attempts, temporary account lockout\n   - Contingency: Monitor failed login attempts and alert on suspicious patterns\n\n## Alternative Approaches\n\n1. **Session-Based Authentication**\n   - Description: Use traditional server-side sessions with cookies instead of JWT\n   - Pros: Easier to invalidate sessions, better for server-rendered applications, no token size limitations\n   - Cons: Requires session storage (Redis/database), harder to scale horizontally, not suitable for APIs consumed by multiple clients\n   - Recommendation: Not chosen - JWT better suits stateless API architecture\n\n2. **OAuth 2.0 / Third-Party Authentication**\n   - Description: Use OAuth providers (Google, GitHub) for authentication instead of custom system\n   - Commands are modular workflows that can be invoked to perform specific tasks.\n\n## File Location\n\n**CRITICAL**: All command files must be created in the `<cwd>/.forge/commands` directory, where `<cwd>` is the current working directory of your code-forge project.\n\n- **Directory**: `<cwd>/.forge/commands`\n- **File format**: `{command-name}.md`\n- **Example**: If your project is at `/home/user/my-project`, commands go in `/home/user/my-project/.forge/commands/`\n\nThis is the only location where forge will discover and load custom commands.\n\n## Command File Structure\n\nEvery command file must have:\n\n1. **YAML Frontmatter** (required):\n   - `name`: Command identifier (use hyphens for multi-word names)\n   - `description`: What the command does\n\n2. **Command Body** (required):\n   - List of steps to execute\n   - Special tags for automated workflows\n   - Clear instructions for each step\n\n### Example Command File\n\n```markdown\n---\nname: check\ndescription: Checks if the code is ready to be committed\n---\n\n- Run the `lint` and `test` commands and verify if everything is fine.\n  <lint>cargo +nightly fmt --all; The system should support user registration, login, logout, and token refresh capabilities while maintaining security best practices.\n\n## Implementation Plan\n\n- [ ] 1. Set up authentication dependencies and configuration\n  - Add JWT library (e.g., jsonwebtoken) and bcrypt for password hashing\n  - Configure environment variables for JWT secrets and token expiration\n  - Rationale: Establishes foundation for secure authentication\n  - Dependencies: None - this is the first step\n\n- [ ] 2. Create user model and database schema\n  - Define User entity with fields: id, email, password_hash, created_at, updated_at\n  - Add unique constraint on email field\n  - Create database migration for users table\n  - Rationale: Provides data structure for storing user credentials\n  - Dependencies: Database connection must be configured\n\n- [ ] 3. Implement password hashing service\n  - Create service to hash passwords using bcrypt with appropriate salt rounds\n  - Add password verification function\n  - Include unit tests for hashing and verification\n  - Rationale: Ensures passwords are never stored in plain text\n  - Dependencies: User model must exist\n\n- [ ] 4. Build JWT token generation and validation\n  - Create service to generate JWT tokens with user claims\n  - Implement token verification and decoding logic\n  - Add refresh token functionality with longer expiration\n  - Rationale: Enables stateless authentication and session management\n  - Dependencies: User model and environment configuration\n\n- [ ] 5. Create authentication endpoints\n  - POST /auth/register - User registration with email/password\n  - POST /auth/login - User login returning access and refresh tokens\n  - POST /auth/logout - Invalidate user session\n  - POST /auth/refresh - Generate new access token from refresh token\n  - Rationale: Provides API interface for authentication operations\n  - Dependencies: All services from previous steps\n\n- [ ] 6. Implement authentication middleware\n  - Create middleware to validate JWT tokens on protected routes\n  - Extract user information from valid tokens\n  - Return 401 for invalid or expired tokens\n  - Rationale: Protects routes requiring authentication\n  - Dependencies: JWT validation service\n\n- [ ] 7. Add rate limiting for authentication endpoints\n  - Implement rate limiting on login and registration endpoints\n  - Configure appropriate limits (e.g., 5 attempts per 15 minutes)\n  - Rationale: Prevents brute force attacks\n  - Dependencies: Authentication endpoints must exist\n\n- [ ] 8. Write integration tests for authentication flow\n  - Test complete registration \342\206\222 login \342\206\222 access protected route flow\n  - Test token refresh mechanism\n  - Test error cases (invalid credentials, expired tokens)\n  - Rationale: Ensures entire authentication system works correctly\n  - Dependencies: All implementation steps complete\n\n## Verification Criteria\n\n- User can successfully register with valid email and password\n- User can login and receive valid JWT tokens\n- Protected routes return 401 for unauthenticated requests\n- Protected routes allow access with valid JWT token\n- Tokens expire after configured duration\n- Refresh tokens can generate new access tokens\n- Passwords are hashed and never stored in plain text\n- Rate limiting prevents excessive authentication attempts\n- All unit and integration tests pass\n- Security audit shows no critical vulnerabilities\n\n## Potential Risks and Mitigations\n\n1. **Token Secret Exposure**\n   - Impact: If JWT secret is exposed, attackers can forge valid tokens\n   - Likelihood: Medium\n   - Mitigation: Store secrets in environment variables, never commit to repository, rotate secrets periodically\n   - Pros: Easier to invalidate sessions, better for server-rendered applications, no token size limitations\n   - Cons: Requires session storage (Redis/database), harder to scale horizontally, not suitable for APIs consumed by multiple clients\n   - 419279 read(10, "#!/bin/bash\n\n# Extract active (non-resolved, non-outdated) review comment threads from a PR,\n# each paired with its surrounding code context (diff hunk).\n#\n# Usage:\n#   ./scripts/pr-comments.sh [PR_NUMBER]\n#\n# If PR_NUMBER is omitted, the script resolves the PR for the current branch.\n\nset -euo pipefail\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Resolve PR number\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n  PR_NUMBER=\"$1\"\nelse\n  PR_NUMBER=$(gh pr view --json number -q '.number' 2>/dev/null) || {\n    echo \"error: not on a branch with an open PR \342\200\224 provide a PR number as the first argument.\" >&2\n    exit 1\n  }\nfi\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Resolve repository owner and name for GraphQL variables.\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\nOWNER=$(gh repo view --json owner -q '.owner.login')\nREPO=$(gh repo view --json name -q '.name')\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Fetch review threads via GraphQL.\n# The REST comments endpoint does not expose resolution or outdated status.\n# GraphQL provides isResolved and isOutdated per thread, which lets us skip\n# threads that no longer need action.\n# --paginate follows endCursor automatically; jq -s merges all pages.\n# gh colorizes output even when piped, so strip ANSI escape codes first.\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\nSTRIP_ANSI=$'s/\\033\\\\[[0-9;]*[mGKH]//g'\n\nTHREADS_JSON=$(gh api graphql \\\n  -f query='\n    query($owner: String!, $repo: String!, $pr: Int!, $endCursor: String) {\n      repository(owner: $owner, name: $repo) {\n        pullRequest(number: $pr) {\n          reviewThreads(first: 100, after: $endCursor) {\n            pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor }\n            nodes {\n              isResolved\n              isOutdated\n              comments(first: 50) {\n                nodes {\n                  path\n                  line\n                  body\n                  author { login }\n                  createdAt\n                  diffHunk\n                }\n              }\n            }\n          }\n        }\n      }\n    }\n  ' \\\n  -f owner=\"$OWNER\" \\\n  -f repo=\"$REPO\" \\\n  -F pr=\"$PR_NUMBER\" \\\n  --paginate \\\n  | sed \"$STRIP_ANSI\" \\\n  | jq -s '[.[].data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[] | select(.isResolved == false and .isOutdated == false)]')\n\nTOTAL=$(echo \"$THREADS_JSON\" | jq 'length')\n\nif [[ \"$TOTAL\" -eq 0 ]]; then\n  echo \"No active review comments found for PR #${PR_NUMBER}.\"\n  exit 0\nfi\n\necho \"PR #${PR_NUMBER} \342\200\224 ${TOTAL} active review thread(s)\"\necho \"\"\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Format and print each active thread in a single jq pass.\n# The first comment in the thread carries the diff hunk (code context).\n# All comments in the thread are shown so the full conversation is visible.\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\nSEP=\"$(printf '%0.s\342\224\200' {1..80})\"\n\necho \"$THREADS_JSON\" | jq -r --arg sep \"$SEP\" '\n  .[] |\n  (.comments.nodes[0]) as $first |\n  [\n    $sep,\n    (\"File   : \" + $first.path + \":\" + (($first.line // \"?\") | tostring)),\n    (\"Author : @\" + $first.author.login),\n    (\"Date   : \" + $first.createdAt),\n    \"\",\n    \"-- code context --\",\n    $first.diffHunk,\n    \"\",\n    \"-- comment --\",\n    (.comments.nodes | map(.body) | join(\"\\n\\n---\\n\\n\")),\n    \"\"\n  ] | join(\"\\n\")\n'\n", 3560) = 3560

When the correct resolution isn't clear from the diff, present numbered options to the user.\n\n## Import Conflicts\n\nWhen both branches modify import statements, merge both sets of imports:\n\n### }\n\n#[test]\nfn test_user_deletion() { ... }\n```\n\n### Test Setup/Fixtures Conflicts\n\nWhen both branches modify test fixtures, merge the changes:\n\n```\n<<<<<<< HEAD\nfn setup() -> TestContext {\n    TestContext {\n        user: create_test_user(),\n        admin: create_admin(),\n    }\n}\n=======\nfn setup() -> TestContext {\n    TestContext {\n        user: create_test_user(),\n        database: init_test_db(),\n    }\n}\n>>>>>>> branch\n```\n\n**Resolution:**\n\n```\nfn setup() -> TestContext {\n    TestContext {\n        user: create_test_user(),\n        admin: create_admin(),\n        database: init_test_db(),\n    }\n}\n```\n\n**Key principles:**\n- Keep all test cases unless they test the exact same thing\n- Merge test fixtures and setup functions\n- If test names conflict but test different things, rename one\n- Preserve all assertions from both sides\n\n**One-line explanation example**: \"Including all test cases from both branches and merging test fixtures.\"\n\n## Lock File Conflicts\n\nLock files (Cargo.lock, package-lock.json, yarn.lock, etc.) should be regenerated rather than manually resolved.\n\n### Pattern: Regenerate Lock File\n\n```bash\n# For Cargo.lock\ngit checkout --theirs Cargo.lock  # or --ours, either works\ncargo update  # or cargo build\n\n# For package-lock.json\ngit checkout --theirs package-lock.json\nnpm install\n\n# For yarn.lock\ngit checkout --theirs yarn.lock\nyarn install\n\n# For Gemfile.lock\ngit checkout --theirs Gemfile.lock\nbundle install\n\n# For poetry.lock\ngit checkout --theirs poetry.lock\npoetry lock --no-update\n```\n\n**Key principles:**\n- Always regenerate, never manually merge\n- Choose either version (--ours or --theirs), doesn't matter\n- Run the package manager's update/install command\n- The result will include dependencies from both branches\n\n**One-line explanation example**: \"Regenerating lock file with package manager to include dependencies from both branches.\"\n\n## Configuration File Conflicts\n\nConfiguration files often need careful merging of both changes.\n\n### Pattern: Merge Configuration Values\n\n```yaml\n<<<<<<< HEAD\nserver:\n  port: 8080\n  timeout: 30\n  max_connections: 100\n=======\nserver:\n  port: 8080\n  timeout: 60\n  enable_https: true\n>>>>>>> branch\n```\n\n**Resolution:**\n\n```yaml\nserver:\n  port: 8080\n  timeout: 60  # Prefer the newer/safer value\n  max_connections: 100\n  enable_https: true\n```\n\n**Key principles:**\n- Include all configuration keys from both sides\n- When same key has different values, choose based on:\n  - Newer value (if timestamp available)\n  - Safer/more conservative value\n  - Production-ready value\n  - Document the choice in commit message\n\n**One-line explanation example**: \"Merging all config keys and choosing incoming value for 'timeout' as it's more recent.\"\n\n**When to ask the user**: If conflicting values have significant implications (e.g., security settings, API endpoints), present options:\n```\nConfig conflict in config.yaml for key 'timeout':\n\n**Option 1**: Keep current value (30 seconds)\n**Option 2**: Keep incoming value (60 seconds)\n**Option 3**: Provide a different value\n\nPlease select an option.\n```\n\n## Code Logic Conflicts\n\nWhen both branches modify the same function, carefully analyze the intent.\n\n### Pattern: Sequential Changes\n\nIf Colors\nRED='\\033[0;31m'\nGREEN='\\033[0;32m'\nYELLOW='\\033[1;33m'\nBLUE='\\033[0;34m'\nNC='\\033[0m'\n\nBACKUP_DIR=\".git/conflict-backups/$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)\"\n\n# Check if we're in a git repository\nif ! git rev-parse --git-dir > /dev/null 2>&1; then\n    echo -e \"${RED}Error: Not a git repository${NC}\" >&2\n    exit 1\nfi\n\n# Find files with delete/modify conflicts\nfind_deleted_modified() {\n    git status --porcelain | grep -E '^(DU|UD|DD|UA|AU|AA)' || true\n}\n\n# Get the content from the branch that modified the file\nget_modified_content() {\n    local file=\"$1\"\n    local status=\"$2\"\n    \n    case \"$status\" in\n        DU) # Deleted by us, modified by them\n            git show \":3:$file\" 2>/dev/null || echo \"\"\n            ;;\n        UD) # Deleted by them, modified by us\n            git show \":2:$file\" 2>/dev/null || echo \"\"\n            ;;\n        *) \n            echo \"\"\n            ;;\n    esac\n}\n\n# Main \"$file\")\n        base_name=\"${filename%.*}\"\n        extension=\"${filename##*.}\"\n        \n        echo -e \"  ${BLUE}Searching for potential relocation targets...${NC}\"\n        \n        # No obvious relocation target found${NC}\"\n            echo -e \"  ${YELLOW}\342\232\240 Changes may need to be manually integrated${NC}\"\n        fi\n        \n        # Create an analysis file\n        analysis_file=\"$BACKUP_DIR/$file.analysis.txt\"\n        cat > \"$analysis_file\" << EOF\nFile: $file\nStatus: $status\nConflict Type: $([ \"$status\" = \"DU\" ] && echo \"Deleted by us, modified by them\" || echo \"Deleted by them, modified by us\")\n\nBacked up to: $backup_file\n\nPotential Actions:\n1. If the file was renamed/moved: Apply changes to the new location\n2. If the file was deleted intentionally: Review if changes are still needed\n3. If the file was refactored: Distribute changes to new file structure\n\nPotential Relocation Targets:\n$similar_files\n\nTo view the changes:\n  cat \"$backup_file\"\n\nTo compare with similar files:\n$(echo \"$similar_files\" | while read -r sf; do echo \"  diff \\\"$backup_file\\\" \\\"$sf\\\"\"; done)\nEOF\n        \n        echo -e \"  ${GREEN}\342\234\223${NC} Analysis saved to: $analysis_file\"\n    else\n        echo -e \"  ${RED}\342\234\227${NC} Could not retrieve content\"\n    fi\n    \n    # Resolve by removing (user must manually apply changes)\n    if [[ \"$status\" == \"DU\" ]]; then\n        git rm \"$file\" 2>/dev/null || true\n        echo -e \"  ${GREEN}\342\234\223${NC} Marked as deleted (ours)\"\n    elif [[ \"$status\" == \"UD\" ]]; then\n        git add \"$file\" 2>/dev/null || git rm \"$file\" 2>/dev/null || true\n        echo -e \"  ${GREEN}\342\234\223${NC} Resolved conflict\"\n    fi\n    \n    echo \"\"\ndone <<< \"$deleted_modified\"\n\n# Create a summary file\nsummary_file=\"$BACKUP_DIR/SUMMARY.md\"\ncat > \"$summary_file\" << EOF\n# Conflict Resolution Summary\n\nGenerated: $(date)\n\n## Deleted-Modified Files Processed\n\n$(echo \"$deleted_modified\" | while IFS= read -r line; do\n    status=\"${line:0:2}\"\n    file=\"${line:3}\"\n    echo \"- **$file** (status: $status)\"\ndone)\n\n## Next Steps\n\n1. Review each backup file in this directory\n2. Identify where the changes should be applied\n3. Manually integrate the changes into the appropriate files\n4. Run tests to validate the integration\n5. Commit the resolved changes\n\n## Files Structure\n\n$(find \"$BACKUP_DIR\" -type f -name \"*.analysis.txt\" | while read -r f; do\n    file=$(basename \"$f\" .analysis.txt)\n    echo \"- \\`$file\\`\"\n    echo \"  - Backup: \\`$file\\`\"\n    echo \"  - Analysis: \\`$file.analysis.txt\\`\"\ndone)\n\nEOF\n\necho -e \"${GREEN}\342\234\223 Summary created: $summary_file${NC}\"\necho \"\"\necho -e \"${BLUE}\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220${NC}\"\necho -e \"${GREEN}\342\234\223 All deleted-but-modified files backed up successfully${NC}\"\necho -e \"${BLUE}\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220\342\225\220${NC}\"\necho \"\"\necho \"Next steps:\"\necho \"  1. 419279 read(10, "---\nname: write-release-notes\ndescription: Generate engaging, high-energy release notes for a given version tag. Fetches the release from GitHub, retrieves every linked PR's title and description, then synthesizes all changes into a polished, user-facing release note with an enthusiastic tone. Use when the user asks to write, generate, or create release notes for a version (e.g. \"write release notes for v1.32.0\", \"generate release notes for the latest release\", \"create changelog for v2.0\").\n---\n\n# Write Release Notes\n\nGenerate clear, informative, and enthusiastic release notes by pulling live data from GitHub and synthesizing every PR into a cohesive narrative.\n\n## Workflow\n\n### 1. Fetch Release Data\n\nRun the bundled script to pull the release metadata and all linked PR details in one shot:\n\n```bash\nbash .forge/skills/write-release-notes/scripts/fetch-release-data.sh <version> [owner/repo]\n```\n\n- `<version>`: The release tag (e.g. `v1.32.0`)\n- `[owner/repo]`: Optional. Defaults to the current repo detected via `gh repo view`.\n\nThe script outputs two sections:\n- `### RELEASE METADATA ###` \342\200\224 tag name, publish date, release name, raw body\n- `### PR DETAILS ###` \342\200\224 one JSON object per PR with: `number`, `title`, `body`, `labels`, `author`, `mergedAt`, `url`\n\n### 2. Categorize Changes\n\nGroup PRs by their conventional commit prefix or label:\n\n| Category | Prefixes / Labels |\n|---|---|\n| Features | `feat`, `type: feature` |\n| Bug Fixes | `fix`, `type: fix` |\n| Performance | `perf` |\n| Refactors | `refactor` |\n| Maintenance | `chore`, `docs`, `ci`, `build`, `deps` |\n\nDependency bumps (e.g. Dependabot PRs) go into Maintenance. Skip PRs with `error: \"not found\"`.\n\n### 3. Write the Release Notes\n\nProduce a Markdown document with the following structure. Keep the tone **informative and enthusiastic** \342\200\224 explain what changed and why it matters, without resorting to marketing fluff.\n\n```markdown\n# [Product Name] [Version] \342\200\224 [Descriptive Tagline]\n\n> One-sentence summary of what this release focuses on.\n\n## What's New\n\n[2-4 sentence narrative covering the biggest features and fixes. \nDescribe what changed and what users can now do. Use active voice. Be factual but upbeat.]\n\n## Highlights\n\n### [Feature/Fix Category]\n**[PR Title rephrased as a clear description of the change]**\n[1-2 sentences expanding on the PR description. Explain what changed and what users can now do differently. \nIf the PR body has useful context, distill it. If empty, infer from the title.]\n\n[Repeat for each significant PR \342\200\224 skip pure chores/dep bumps unless noteworthy]\n\n## Bug Fixes & Reliability\n\n[Bullet list of fixes, each with a brief impact statement]\n\n## Under the Hood\n\n[Brief paragraph or bullet list covering refactors, maintenance, and dep updates \342\200\224 \nkeep it light, acknowledge the work without boring the reader]\n\n## Contributors\n\nA huge thank you to everyone who made this release happen: [list @handles \342\200\224 exclude bots like @dependabot]\n\n---\n**Full changelog**: [GitHub Release link]\n```\n\n### 4. Tone & Style Guidelines\n\n- **Lead with what changed**: \"You can now...\" or \"Forge now...\" beats \"We added...\"\n- **Be specific**: Name the feature and describe what it does, not just the category\n- **Be informative, not marketty**: Avoid vague adjectives like \"seamless\", \"smarter\", \"blazing\", \"powerful\", \"rock-solid\". Instead, state the concrete fact (e.g. \"editor no longer spawns a git process on every keystroke\" beats \"blazing-fast editor\")\n- **Enthusiasm through substance**: Let the actual improvement speak for itself. Use active, direct language.\n- **Short paragraphs**: Max 3 sentences per block\n- **Skip internal jargon**: Translate crate names and internal concepts into plain language\n- **Celebrate contributors**: Name them by handle\n- **Tagline formula**: `[Version] \342\200\224 [Factual Theme Description]` (e.g. \"v1.32.0 \342\200\224 Terminal Context, File Drop Support, Windows Performance\")\n- **No implementation details**: Do not mention internal module names, struct names, function names, crate names, or how something was implemented. Focus purely on what the user experiences or gains.\n- **No PR/issue references**: Do not include PR numbers, issue numbers, or links to GitHub PRs/issues in the release notes. Focus on the changes themselves, not their tracking identifiers.\n\n### 5. Validate Length\n\nAfter writing the release notes, run the bundled validation script to confirm the output is under 2000 characters:\n\n```bash\necho \"<release notes>\" | bash .forge/skills/write-release-notes/scripts/validate-release-notes.sh\n```\n\nIf it prints `FAIL`, trim the draft and re-run until it prints `PASS`:\n- Remove the Under the Hood section first\n- Consolidate Bug Fixes into a shorter bullet list\n- Shorten individual PR descriptions to one tight sentence\n- Remove the least impactful Highlights entries\n\n### 7. Output\n\nPrint the final release notes directly in the chat. 419279 read(10, "# Bounty Automation\n\nAutomates the full lifecycle of issue bounties \342\200\224 from label propagation when a PR is opened, through claiming when work begins, to rewarding when a PR is merged.\n\n## Flow\n\n```\nIssue created\n\342\224\224\342\224\200\342\224\200 maintainer adds  bounty: $N  label\n        \342\224\202\n        \342\224\234\342\224\200\342\224\200 parse-sync-generic-bounty.ts  \342\206\222  adds generic  bounty  label\n        \342\224\202\n        \342\226\274\nIssue assigned to contributor\n\342\224\224\342\224\200\342\224\200 parse-sync-claimed.ts  \342\206\222  adds  bounty: claimed\n        \342\224\202\n        \342\226\274\nContributor opens PR with \"Closes #N\" / \"Fixes #N\" / \"Resolves #N\"\n\342\224\224\342\224\200\342\224\200 parse-propagate-label.ts  \342\206\222  copies  bounty: $N  to PR\n                              \342\206\222  posts comment on issue: \"PR #X opened by @author\"\n        \342\224\202\n        \342\226\274\nPR is merged\n\342\224\224\342\224\200\342\224\200 parse-mark-rewarded.ts  \342\206\222  adds  bounty: rewarded  to PR\n                            \342\206\222  adds  bounty: rewarded  to linked issue(s)\n                            \342\206\222  removes  bounty: claimed  from linked issue(s)\n        \342\224\202\n        \342\226\274\nBounty lifecycle complete\n\nRemoval path:\nmaintainer removes last  bounty: $N  label\n\342\224\224\342\224\200\342\224\200 parse-sync-generic-bounty.ts  \342\206\222  removes generic  bounty  label\n```\n\n## Labels\n\n| Label                            | Applied to | Set by                                                      |\n| -------------------------------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `bounty: $100` \342\200\246 `bounty: $5500` | Issue      | Maintainer (manually)                                       |\n| `bounty`                         | Issue      | `parse-sync-generic-bounty.ts` on value label add/remove    |\n| `bounty: claimed`                | Issue      | `parse-sync-claimed.ts` on assignment                       |\n| `bounty: rewarded`               | Issue + PR | `parse-mark-rewarded.ts` on merge                           |\n\nBounty values follow the Fibonacci sequence: **$100, $200, $300, $500, $800, $1300, $2100, $3400, $5500**.\n\n## Pipeline\n\nEach workflow job runs a single Node process (`run.ts`) that executes all three stages in memory \342\200\224 no temp files, no shell piping:\n\n```\nparse  \342\206\222  ParsedIntent (in memory)  \342\206\222  plan  \342\206\222  BatchPlan (in memory)  \342\206\222  execute\n```\n\n**Stage 1 \342\200\224 parse** (`parse-*.ts`): Reads the GitHub Actions event payload from `GITHUB_EVENT_PATH` and returns a `ParsedIntent` object. Pure \342\200\224 makes no API calls.\n\n**Stage 2 \342\200\224 plan** (`plan.ts`): Receives the `ParsedIntent`, fetches current labels only for targets not already known from the event payload, diffs desired vs actual state, and returns a `BatchPlan`. Minimises API calls by reusing label data already present in the event.\n\n**Stage 3 \342\200\224 execute** (`execute.ts`): Receives the `BatchPlan` and applies all mutations. Label additions per target are sent as a single batched `POST /labels` call. Each removal is a separate `DELETE` (GitHub has no bulk-remove endpoint). Comments are posted last.\n\nThis design means:\n- The parse stage is trivially unit-testable (pure function, no mocks needed).\n- The plan stage is testable with a minimal mock that only needs `getLabels`.\n- The execute stage is testable with a mock that tracks calls \342\200\224 no HTTP.\n- API calls are minimised: additions are batched per target; label state already in the event payload is never re-fetched.\n\n## Scripts\n\nThe workflow invokes a single orchestrator script (`run.ts`) per job. The parse, plan, and execute modules are called directly in the same Node process, passing objects in memory.\n\n### `run.ts`\n\nThe entrypoint used by `bounty.yml`. Accepts a `--script` flag to select which parse module to run, then calls `plan` and `execute` in sequence \342\200\224 all in-process.\n\n```sh\nnpx tsx .github/scripts/bounty/run.ts \\\n  --script <parse-script> \\\n  --repo <owner/repo> \\\n  --token <github-token> \\\n  [--pr <number> | --issue <number>]\n```\n\n### `parse-propagate-label.ts`\n\nTriggered by: `pull_request` \342\200\224 opened, edited, reopened.\n\n1. Parses the PR body for closing keywords (`closes`, `fixes`, `resolves`, case-insensitive).\n2. Returns a `ParsedIntent` with a `labelCopies` field \342\200\224 the plan stage fetches each linked issue's labels and copies any `bounty: $N` ones onto the PR.\n3. Includes a comment mutation per linked issue (the plan stage drops it if the issue has no bounty labels).\n\n### `parse-sync-claimed.ts`\n\nTriggered by: `issues` \342\200\224 assigned, unassigned.\n\n- **assigned**: returns `add: [\"bounty: claimed\"]` if the issue has a `bounty: $N` label.\n- **unassigned**: returns `remove: [\"bounty: claimed\"]` only when no assignees remain.\n- Issue labels are already in the event payload and supplied as `knownLabels` \342\200\224 no extra fetch.\n\n### `parse-sync-generic-bounty.ts`\n\nTriggered by: `issues` \342\200\224 labeled, unlabeled.\n\nKeeps the generic `bounty` label in sync with value labels. Inspects `event.label` (the label that just changed) and only acts when it matches `bounty: $`.\n\n- **labeled**: returns `add: [\"bounty\"]`.\n- **unlabeled**: returns `remove: [\"bounty\"]` only when no value labels remain (guards against mid-tier-swap removal when a maintainer swaps one value label for another).\n- Issue labels from the event are supplied as `knownLabels` \342\200\224 no extra fetch.\n\n### `parse-mark-rewarded.ts`\n\nTriggered by: `pull_request_target` \342\200\224 closed (merged only).\n\n1. Returns empty intent if the PR was not merged or has no `bounty: $N` label.\n2. Returns `add: [\"bounty: rewarded\"]` for the PR (labels known from event, no fetch).\n3. Parses the PR body for linked issues; returns `add: [\"bounty: rewarded\"], remove: [\"bounty: claimed\"]` for each (plan stage fetches their labels).\n\nUses `pull_request_target` so the job has write access to issues and PRs from forks.\n\n### `plan.ts`\n\nReceives a `ParsedIntent` from the parse stage. Resolves `labelCopies` by fetching source issue labels. Fetches current labels for any target not already in `knownLabels`. Filters out no-op adds and removes. Returns a `BatchPlan`.\n\n### `execute.ts`\n\nReceives a `BatchPlan` from the plan stage. For each mutation: one batched `POST` for all additions, one `DELETE` per removal, one `POST` per comment.\n\n## Shared Module\n\n`github-api.ts` defines:\n- Event payload types (`PullRequestEvent`, `IssuesEvent`)\n- Pipeline types (`ParsedIntent`, `BatchPlan`, `TargetMutation`)\n- The `GitHubApi` interface (injectable for testing)\n- `GitHubRestApi` \342\200\224 the production implementation using `node:https`\n\nAll scripts import types from `github-api.ts` and accept a `GitHubApi` instance in their `run()` / `plan()` / `execute()` function signature, making every step independently mockable.\n\n## Tests\n\nUnit tests live alongside each script (`*.test.ts`) and use Node's built-in `node:test` runner.\n\n```sh\nnpm run test:bounty\n```\n\n- Parse tests: pure \342\200\224 no mock needed, just call `parse()` with a synthetic event.\n- Plan and execute tests: use a mock `GitHubApi` that tracks calls and returns preset label lists.\n- The CLI entrypoint in each script (yargs parsing + `GITHUB_EVENT_PATH` read) is guarded behind an `import.meta.url` check so it does not execute on import.\n\n## Workflow Source\n\n`bounty.yml` is auto-generated from Rust source in `crates/forge_ci`. 419279 read(10, "# Agent Guidelines\n\nThis document contains guidelines and best practices for AI agents working with this codebase.\n\n## Error Management\n\n- Use `anyhow::Result` for error handling in services and repositories.\n- Create domain errors using `thiserror`.\n- Never implement `From` for converting domain errors, manually convert them\n\n## Writing Tests\n\n- All tests should be written in three discrete steps:\n\n  ```rust,ignore\n  use pretty_assertions::assert_eq; // Always use pretty assertions\n\n  fn test_foo() {\n      let setup = ...; // Instantiate a fixture or setup for the test\n      let actual = ...; // Execute the fixture to create an output\n      let expected = ...; // Define a hand written expected result\n      assert_eq!(actual, expected); // Assert that the actual result matches the expected result\n  }\n  ```\n\n- Use `pretty_assertions` for better error messages.\n\n- Use fixtures to create test data.\n\n- Use `assert_eq!` for equality checks.\n\n- Use `assert!(...)` for boolean checks.\n\n- Use unwraps in test functions and anyhow::Result in fixtures.\n\n- Keep the boilerplate to a minimum.\n\n- Use words like `fixture`, `actual` and `expected` in test functions.\n\n- Fixtures should be generic and reusable.\n\n- Test should always be written in the same file as the source code.\n\n- Use `new`, Default and derive_setters::Setters to create `actual`, `expected` and specially `fixtures`. For example:\n\n  **Good:**\n\n  ```rust,ignore\n  User::default().age(12).is_happy(true).name(\"John\")\n  User::new(\"Job\").age(12).is_happy()\n  User::test() // Special test constructor\n  ```\n\n  **Bad:**\n\n  ```rust,ignore\n  User {name: \"John\".to_string(), is_happy: true, age: 12}\n  User::with_name(\"Job\") // Bad name, should stick to User::new() or User::test()\n  ```\n\n- Use `unwrap()` unless the error information is useful. Use `expect` instead of `panic!` when error message is useful. For example:\n\n  **Good:**\n\n  ```rust,ignore\n  users.first().expect(\"List should not be empty\")\n  ```\n\n  **Bad:**\n\n  ```rust,ignore\n  if let Some(user) = users.first() {\n      // ...\n  } else {\n      panic!(\"List should not be empty\")\n  }\n  ```\n\n- Prefer using `assert_eq` on full objects instead of asserting each field:\n\n  **Good:**\n\n  ```rust,ignore\n  assert_eq!(actual, expected);\n  ```\n\n  **Bad:**\n\n  ```rust,ignore\n  assert_eq!(actual.a, expected.a);\n  assert_eq!(actual.b, expected.b);\n  ```\n\n## Verification\n\nAlways verify changes by running tests and linting the codebase\n\n1. Run crate specific tests to ensure they pass.\n\n   ```\n   cargo insta test --accept\n   ```\n\n2. **Build Guidelines**:\n   - **NEVER** run `cargo build --release` unless absolutely necessary (e.g., performance testing, creating binaries for distribution)\n   - For verification, use `cargo check` (fastest), `cargo insta test`, or `cargo build` (debug mode)\n   - Release builds take significantly longer and are rarely needed for development verification\n\n## Writing Domain Types\n\n- Use `derive_setters` to derive setters and use the `strip_option` and the `into` attributes on the struct types.\n\n## Documentation\n\n- **Always** write Rust docs (`///`) for all public methods, functions, structs, enums, and traits.\n- Document parameters with `# Arguments` and errors with `# Errors` sections when applicable.\n- **Do not include code examples** - docs are for LLMs, not humans. Focus on clear, concise functionality descriptions.\n\n## Refactoring\n\n- If asked to fix failing tests, always confirm whether to update the implementation or the tests.\n\n## Git Operations\n\n- Safely assume git is pre-installed\n- Safely assume github cli (gh) is pre-installed\n- Always use `Co-Authored-By: ForgeCode <noreply@forgecode.dev>` for git commits and Github comments\n\n## Service Implementation Guidelines\n\nServices should follow clean architecture principles and maintain clear separation of concerns:\n\n### Core Principles\n\n- **No service-to-service dependencies**: Services should never depend on other services directly\n- **Infrastructure dependency**: Services should depend only on infrastructure abstractions when needed\n- **Single type parameter**: Services should take at most one generic type parameter for infrastructure\n- **No trait objects**: Avoid `Box<dyn ...>` - use concrete types and generics instead\n- **Constructor pattern**: Implement `new()` without type bounds - apply bounds only on methods that need them\n- **Compose dependencies**: Use the `+` operator to combine multiple infrastructure traits into a single bound\n- **Arc<T> for Service<T>(Arc<T>)`\n\n### Examples\n\n#### Simple Service (No Infrastructure)\n\n```rust,ignore\npub struct UserValidationService;\n\nimpl UserValidationService {\n    pub fn new() -> Self { ... }\n\n    pub fn validate_email(&self, email: &str) -> Result<()> {\n        // Validation logic here\n        ...\n    }\n\n    pub fn validate_age(&self, age: u32) -> Result<()> {\n        // Age validation logic here\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n#### Service with Infrastructure Dependency\n\n```rust,ignore\n// Infrastructure trait (defined in infrastructure layer)\npub trait UserRepository UserService<R> {\n    // Business logic methods have type bounds where needed\n    pub fn create_user(&self, email: &str, name: &str) -> Result<User> { ... }\n    pub fn find_user(&self, email: &str) -> Result<Option<User>> { ... }\n}\n```\n\n#### Tuple Struct Pattern for Simple Services\n\n```rust,ignore\n// Infrastructure traits\npub trait FileReader {\n    async fn read_file(&self, path: &Path) -> Result<String>;\n}\n\npub trait Environment {\n    fn max_file_size(&self) -> u64;\n}\n\n// Tuple struct for simple single dependency service\npub struct FileService<F>(Arc<F>);\n\nimpl<F> FileService<F> {\n    // Constructor without bounds\n    pub fn new(infra: Arc<F>) -> Self { ... }\n}\n\nimpl<F: FileReader + Environment> FileService<F> {\n    // Business logic methods with composed trait bounds\n    pub async fn read_with_validation(&self, path: &Path) -> Result<String> { ... }\n}\n```\n\n### Anti-patterns to Avoid\n\n```rust,ignore\n// BAD: Service depending on another service\npub struct BadUserService<R, E> {\n    repository: R,\n    email_service: E, // Don't do this!\n}\n\n// BAD: Using trait objects\npub struct BadUserService {\n    repository: Box<dyn UserRepository>, // Avoid Box<dyn>\n}\n\n// BAD: Multiple infrastructure dependencies with separate type parameters\npub struct BadUserService<R, C, L> {\n    repository: R,\n    cache: C,\n    logger: L, // Too many generic parameters - hard to use and test\n}\n\nimpl<R: UserRepository, C: Cache, L: Logger> BadUserService<R, C, L> {\n    // BAD: Constructor with type bounds makes it hard to use\n    pub fn new(repository: R, cache: C, logger: L) -> Self { ... }\n}\n\n// BAD: Usage becomes cumbersome\nlet service = BadUserService::<PostgresRepo, RedisCache, FileLogger>::new(...);\n```\n", Alternatively, you can configure providers beforehand:\n\n```bash\n# Configure your provider credentials interactively\nforge provider login\n\n# Then start Forge\nforge\n```\nThat's it! Forge is now ready to assist you with your development tasks.\n\n## Usage Examples\n\nForge can be used in different ways depending on your needs. Here are some common usage patterns:\n\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Code Understanding</strong></summary>\n\n```\n> Can you explain how the authentication system works in this codebase?\n```\n\nForge will analyze your project's structure, identify authentication-related files, and provide a detailed explanation of the authentication flow, including the relationships between different components.\n\n</details>\n\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Implementing New Features</strong></summary>\n\n```\n> I need to add a dark mode toggle to our React application. How should I approach this?\n```\n\nForge will suggest the best approach based on your current codebase, explain the steps needed, and even scaffold the necessary components and styles for you.\n\n</details>\n\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Debugging Assistance</strong></summary>\n\n```\n> I'm getting this error: \"TypeError: Cannot read property 'map' of undefined\". What might be causing it?\n```\n\nForge will analyze the error, suggest potential causes based on your code, and propose different solutions to fix the issue.\n\n</details>\n\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Code Reviews</strong></summary>\n\n```\n> Please review the code in src/components/UserProfile.js and suggest improvements\n```\n\nForge will analyze the code, identify potential issues, and suggest improvements for readability, performance, security, and maintainability.\n\n</details>\n\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Learning New Technologies</strong></summary>\n\n```\n> I want to integrate GraphQL into this Express application. Can you explain how to get started?\n```\n\nForge will provide a tailored tutorial on integrating GraphQL with Express, using your specific project structure as context.\n\n</details>\n\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Database Schema Design</strong></summary>\n\n```\n> I need to design a database schema for a blog with users, posts, comments, and categories\n```\n\nForge will suggest an appropriate schema design, including tables/collections, relationships, indexes, and constraints based on your project's existing database technology.\n\n</details>\n\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Refactoring Legacy Code</strong></summary>\n\n```\n> Help me refactor this class-based component to use React Hooks\n```\n\nForge can help modernize your codebase by walking you through refactoring steps and implementing them with your approval.\n\n</details>\n\n<details>\n<summary><strong>Git Operations</strong></summary>\n\n```\n> I need to merge branch 'feature/user-profile' into main but there are conflicts\n```\n\nForge can guide you through resolving git conflicts, explaining the differences and suggesting the best way to reconcile them.\n\n</details>\n\n## Why Forge?\n\nForge is designed for developers who want to enhance their workflow with AI assistance while maintaining full control over their development environment.\n\n- **Zero configuration** - Just add your API key and you're ready to go\n- **Seamless integration** - Works right in your terminal, where you already work\n- **Multi-provider support** - Use OpenAI, Anthropic, or other LLM providers\n- **Secure by design** - Restricted shell mode limits file system access and prevents unintended changes\n- **Open-source** - Transparent, extensible, and community-driven\n\nForge helps you code faster, solve complex problems, and learn new technologies without leaving your terminal.\n\n---\n\n## How Forge Works: Three Modes\n\nForge has three distinct ways to use it. Understanding this distinction upfront will save you confusion.\n\n### Interactive Mode (TUI)\n\nRunning `forge` with no arguments starts the interactive terminal UI, a persistent session where you type prompts and the AI responds in a conversational loop. This is the primary way to do multi-step work.\n\n```bash\nforge                              # Start a new interactive session\nforge conversation resume <id>     # Resume a specific saved conversation in interactive mode\nforge --conversation-id <id>       # Same: resume conversation by ID\nforge --agent <agent-id>           # Start interactive session with a specific agent\nforge -C /path/to/project          # Start in a specific directory\nforge --sandbox experiment-name    # Create an isolated git worktree + branch, then start there\n```\n\nOnce inside interactive mode, type your prompt and press Enter. Forge reads files, writes patches, runs commands, and maintains context across the whole session.\n\n### One-Shot CLI Mode\n\nPass `-p` (or `--prompt`) to run a single prompt and exit. Forge does the work and returns to your shell. Useful for scripts, piping output, or quick tasks.\n\n```bash\nforge -p \"Explain the purpose of src/main.rs\"\nforge -p \"Add error handling to the parse() function in lib.rs\"\necho \"What does this do?\" | forge    # Pipe input as the prompt\nforge commit                         # Generate an AI commit message and commit (exits when done)\nforge commit --preview               # Generate commit message, print it, then exit\nforge suggest \"find large log files\" # Translate natural language to a shell command, then exit\n```\n\n> **Note:** `forge conversation resume <id>` opens the interactive TUI. It does **not** just print a message and exit. If you run it and see the cursor waiting, you are inside the interactive session. Type your prompt or press `Ctrl+C` to exit.\n\n### ZSH Plugin Mode (`:` prefix)\n\nInstall the ZSH plugin once with `forge setup`, then use `:` commands directly at your shell prompt without ever typing `forge`. This is the fastest mode for day-to-day development: send prompts, switch conversations, commit, and suggest commands without leaving your shell.\n\n```zsh\n: refactor the auth module      # Send a prompt to the active agent\n:commit                         # AI-powered git commit\n:suggest \"find large log files\" # Translate description \342\206\222 shell command in your buffer\n:conversation                   # Browse saved conversations with interactive picker\n```\n\nSee the full [ZSH Plugin reference below](#zsh-plugin-the--prefix-system) for all commands and aliases.\n\n---\n\n## ZSH Plugin: The `:` Prefix System\n\nWhen you install the ZSH plugin (`forge setup`), you get a `:` prefix command system at your shell prompt. This is the fastest way to use Forge during normal development; you never leave your shell.\n\n**How it works:** Lines starting with `:` are intercepted before the shell sees them and routed to Forge. Everything else runs normally.\n\n```zsh\n: <prompt>         # Send a prompt to the active agent\n:sage <prompt>     # Send a prompt to a specific agent by name (sage, muse, forge, or any custom agent)\n:agent <name>      # Switch the active agent; opens interactive picker if no name given\n```\n\n### Agents\n\nForge ships with three built-in agents, each with a different role:\n\n| Agent | Alias | Purpose | Modifies files? |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `forge` | (default) | Implementation: builds features, fixes"..., 45645) = 45645

The `forgee` symlink provides a stable absolute path that works from any directory.\n\n### Running Evaluations\n\n```bash\n# Run an evaluation\nnpm run eval ./evals/create_skill/task.yml\n\n# Set custom log level\nLOG_LEVEL=debug npm run eval ./evals/create_skill/task.yml\n```\n\n## How It Works\n\nThe evaluation system executes commands based on task definitions and validates their output. It supports:\n\n- **Parallel execution** with configurable concurrency\n- **Timeout handling** for long-running tasks\n- **Data-driven testing** using CSV files\n- **Output validation** using regex patterns\n- **Debug artifacts** stored with timestamps\n\n## Project Structure\n\n```\nbenchmarks/\n\342\224\234\342\224\200\342\224\200 cli.ts                    # Main CLI entry point\n\342\224\234\342\224\200\342\224\200 command-generator.ts      # Command template rendering\n\342\224\234\342\224\200\342\224\200 task-executor.ts          # Task execution with timeout support\n\342\224\234\342\224\200\342\224\200 model.ts                  # TypeScript types for tasks\n\342\224\234\342\224\200\342\224\200 parse.ts                  # CLI argument parsing\n\342\224\224\342\224\200\342\224\200 evals/                    # Evaluation definitions\n    \342\224\224\342\224\200\342\224\200 create_skill/\n        \342\224\234\342\224\200\342\224\200 task.yml          # Task definition\n        \342\224\234\342\224\200\342\224\200 create_skill_tasks.csv  # Test data\n        \342\224\224\342\224\200\342\224\200 debug/            # Debug outputs (timestamped)\n```\n\n## Creating an Evaluation\n\n### 1. Create an Evaluation Directory\n\n```bash\nmkdir -p evals/my_eval\n```\n\n### 2. Create a `task.yml` File\n\nThe task file defines how to run your evaluation:\n\n```yaml\n# Optional: Commands to run before evaluation starts\nbefore_run:\n  - cargo build\n  - npm install\n\n# Required: Command(s) to execute for each test case\n# Single command\nrun: forgee -p '{{prompt}}'\n\n# Or multiple commands (executed sequentially)\nrun:\n  - echo \"Step 1: {{task}}\"\n  - forgee -p '{{prompt}}'\n  - echo \"Step 2: Complete\"\n\n# Execution configuration\nparallelism: 10  # Number of tasks to run in parallel (default: 1)\ntimeout: 60      # Timeout in seconds (optional)\nearly_exit: true # Stop execution when validations pass (optional)\n\n# Optional: Validations to run on output\nvalidations:\n  - name: \"Check success message\"\n    type: regex\n    regex: \\[[0-9:]*\\] Skill create-skill\n\n# Required: Data sources for test cases\nsources:\n  - csv: my_tasks.csv\n```\n\n#### Task File Schema\n\n**`before_run`** (optional): Array of shell commands to execute before running tasks\n- Runs sequentially before the main command execution\n- Executes in a temporary directory created for the evaluation run\n- Useful for building binaries or setting up dependencies\n\n**`run`** (required): Command(s) to execute for each test case\n- Can be a single string or an array of strings\n- Commands support template placeholders (e.g., `{{variable}}`)\n- Multiple commands are executed sequentially\n- If any command fails, subsequent commands are skipped\n\n**`parallelism`** (optional): Number of tasks to run concurrently (default: 1)\n\n**`timeout`** (optional): Maximum execution time in seconds per task\n\n**`early_exit`** (optional): Stop command execution when all validations pass\n\n**`validations`** (optional): Array of validation rules\n- `name`: Human-readable description\n- `type`: Validation type. Supported values:\n  - `regex`: Match output against a regular expression pattern\n  - `shell`: Execute a shell command with output as stdin\n- For `regex` type:\n  - `regex`: Regular expression pattern to match in output\n- For `shell` type:\n  - `command`: Shell command to execute (receives task output via stdin)\n  - `exit_code`: Expected exit code (default: 0)\n\n**`sources`** (required): Array of data sources\n- Currently supports CSV files: `- csv: filename.csv`\n- Future: Command output: `- cmd: command`\n\n### 3. Create Test Data (CSV)\n\nCreate a CSV file with columns matching your template variables:\n\n```csv\nprompt,expected_output\n\"Create a backup script\",\"backup.sh\"\n\"Generate API client\",\"api_client.py\"\n```\n\nThe column names (e.g., `prompt`, `expected_output`) become template variables you can use in your command with `{{column_name}}`.\n\n### 4. Run the Evaluation\n\n```bash\nnpm run eval ./evals/my_eval/task.yml\n```\n\n## Template Variables\n\nCommands support Handlebars template syntax. Variables are populated from CSV columns:\n\n```yaml\nrun:\n  command: ./tool --input '{{input_file}}' --format {{format}} --verbose\n```\n\nWith CSV:\n```csv\ninput_file,format\ndata1.txt,json\ndata2.txt,yaml\n```\n\n## Output and Debugging\n\n### Debug Artifacts\n\nEach run creates a timestamped debug directory:\n\n```\nevals/my_eval/debug/2025-11-23T10-30-45-123Z/\n\342\224\234\342\224\200\342\224\200 task-1.log\n\342\224\234\342\224\200\342\224\200 task-2.log\n\342\224\224\342\224\200\342\224\200 task-3.log\n```\n\nEach log file contains the full output (stdout + stderr) from the command execution.\n\n### Task Status\n\nTasks can have four statuses:\n\n- **`passed`**: Task completed successfully and passed all validations\n- **`validation_failed`**: Task completed but failed one or more validations\n- **`timeout`**: Task exceeded the timeout limit\n- **`failed`**: Task execution failed (non-zero exit code)\n\n### Logging\n\n**Human-readable output (default):**\n```bash\nnpm run eval ./evals/my_eval/task.yml\n```\n\n**Machine-readable JSON output:**\n```bash\nLOG_JSON=1 npm run eval ./evals/my_eval/task.yml | jq .\n```\n\n**Debug logging:**\n```bash\nLOG_LEVEL=debug npm run eval ./evals/my_eval/task.yml\n```\n\n## Examples\n\n### Example 1: Simple Sequential Execution\n\n```yaml\nrun: echo \"Processing {{name}}\"\nsources:\n  - csv: names.csv\n```\n\n```csv\nname\nAlice\nBob\nCharlie\n```\n\n### Example 2: Parallel Execution with Timeout\n\n```yaml\nrun: ./slow_task --id {{task_id}}\nparallelism: 5\ntimeout: 30\nsources:\n  - csv: tasks.csv\n```\n\n### Example 3: Multiple Commands\n\n```yaml\nrun:\n  - echo \"Starting task {{id}}\"\n  - ./process --input {{file}}\n  - echo \"Task {{id}} complete\"\nparallelism: 3\ntimeout: 120\nsources:\n  - csv: tasks.csv\n```\n\n### Example 4: Shell Command Validation\n\n```yaml\nrun: echo \"{{message}}\"\nparallelism: 3\nvalidations:\n  # Using grep to check if output contains specific text\n  - name: \"Contains 'test' word\"\n    type: shell\n    command: grep -q \"test\"\n    exit_code: 0\n  \n  # Count words and ensure it's greater than 2\n  - name: \"More than 2 words\"\n    type: shell\n    command: test $(wc -w | awk '{print $1}') -gt 2\n    exit_code: 0\n  \n  # Traditional regex validation (for comparison)\n  - name: \"Contains test or validation\"\n    type: regex\n    regex: \"test|validation\"\nsources:\n  - csv: messages.csv\n```\n\n### Example 5: Regex Validation\n\n```yaml\nrun: cargo test {{test_name}}\nvalidations:\n  - name: \"All tests passed\"\n    type: regex\n    regex: test result:\\s+ok\nsources:\n  - csv: tests.csv\n```\n\n## Tips\n\n1. **Use quotes in commands**: When passing CSV values with spaces, wrap them in quotes:\n   ```yaml\n   command: forge -p '{{prompt}}'\n   ```\n\n2. **Build before running**: Use `before_run` to ensure binaries are up-to-date:\n   ```yaml\n   before_run:\n     - Provider-executed tools need to be identified and converted using the new provider-specific conversion logic before being included in the API request.
